cubes.title: Perspective shrinks an angle, never to zero
cubes.mini: A thing of size s at distance d fills the angle θ = 2 arctan(s/2d): halved when the distance doubles, never zero. A zoom by the ratio of the distances gives back the same picture.
cubes.text: The eye sees angles, not sizes: what is seen under a larger angle appears larger [1]. A thing of size s at distance d fills θ = 2 arctan(s/2d) ≈ s/d. Four 1 m cubes on a square, the lower two on the floor and the upper two from 2 to 3 m, seen from 1.7 m, move from 4 m to 2 km: the gap between the rows falls to {{gap1k}}′ at 1 km and {{gap10k}}′ at 10 km, and is never zero. A picture is a cross-section of the pyramid of straight lines from the eye [2]. The naked eye separates about 1′ [3], reached by a 1 m gap at {{gapAcuity}} km; a zoom by the ratio of the distances gives back the same square, gap included. Eye level stays between the rows: what is above the eye never comes down to it.
cubes.verdict: Would refute the picture: a gap that closes at a finite distance, or a far object above eye level seen below it on a flat floor.
lines.title: Parallel lines meet only at infinity
lines.mini: A pinhole maps (X, Y, Z) to (f X/Z, f Y/Z). A line of direction (a, b, c) ends at (f a/c, f b/c) wherever it starts: parallel lines share one vanishing point; lines parallel to the picture stay parallel.
lines.text: A pinhole or an eye maps a point (X, Y, Z) in front of it to (f X/Z, f Y/Z). Follow a straight line of direction (a, b, c): its image ends at (f a/c, f b/c), whatever its starting point. All lines of one direction therefore run to one point of the picture, which depends only on that direction: the rails meet at the horizon, Alberti's centric point [1]. Lines parallel to the picture (c = 0) never meet; their images stay parallel. Lines going towards the viewer's back run to the opposite point, behind the head.
lines.verdict: Would refute the picture: parallel rails whose images cross before the horizon, or a fence parallel to the picture whose rails converge.
sunset.title: Perspective cannot set a Sun that is above a plane
sunset.mini: A Sun h above a flat Earth is seen at α = arctan(h/d) > 0 at every distance: at 5,000 km up and 20,000 km away it stands {{alphaMin}}° high and shrinks {{deltaRatio}}×. The real Sun keeps 32′ and goes under the horizon.
sunset.text: Flat-earth models put the Sun some 4,800 to 5,500 km above the disc [1]. Seen from a distance d, its height angle is α = arctan(h/d), positive for every d and every h: the sign does not depend on the free parameter. With h = {{sunH}} km, it is still {{alphaMin}}° up at {{dMax}} km, half a meridian; to come down to half a degree it would have to be {{dHalfDeg}} thousand km away. Its apparent diameter δ = D/√(h² + d²) would fall from {{deltaZen}}′ overhead to {{deltaMax}}′. Measured, the Sun's disc is 31.5′ to 32.5′ across through the year [2], the same at noon and at sunset; refraction flattens it vertically near the horizon and leaves its width unchanged [3]. It touches the horizon and goes under it, bottom first.
sunset.verdict: Would vindicate the flat Sun: a disc that shrinks by a factor of a few from noon to evening and stops a whole number of degrees above the horizon.
dip.title: From a mountain, the sky goes below eye level: only on a globe
dip.mini: On a globe the horizon drops by δ = arccos(R/(R + h)) as you climb, {{dip1}}° from 1 km, opening a strip of sky below eye level. On a plane the Sun, Moon and stars, higher than any mountain, stay above it.
dip.text: Perspective keeps above eye level everything higher than the eye. Flat-earth models put the Sun and Moon thousands of kilometres above the disc [1]: from a 2 km summit the flat Sun is still at least {{flatSun2}}° up, and the plane's horizon stays at eye level ({{flatDip2}}″ below it at the edge of the disc). On a globe the horizon sinks by δ = arccos(R/(R + h)) ≈ √(2h/R): {{dip1}}° from 1 km and {{dip2}}° from 2 km ({{dip1k}}° and {{dip2k}}° with standard refraction, k = 0.13). Between eye level and the horizon a strip of sky opens: the Sun 0.75° below eye level shows its top from {{sunRiseTop}} m and its whole disc from {{sunRise}} m, and stars below eye level come out one by one. A spirit level and a theodolite on a summit show which happens.
dip.verdict: Would vindicate the plane: from a summit, a sea horizon on the spirit level's line, and no star, Sun or Moon ever seen below it.
rays.title: Sunbeams are parallel lines, seen in perspective
rays.mini: Shafts of light through gaps in a cloud fan out from the Sun, are parallel when seen side-on, and close up again towards the antisolar point: every beam lies on a great circle through the Sun and its opposite point.
rays.text: Crepuscular rays, the shafts of sunlight through gaps in clouds, fan out from the Sun. They are parallel lines going away from the viewer towards the Sun, so their images meet at their vanishing point, the Sun itself [1]. Side-on they are parallel to the picture and stay parallel. Behind the viewer they run to the opposite vanishing point, the antisolar point, as far below the horizon as the Sun is above it: the anticrepuscular rays [1] [2]. In the animation the cloud is {{cloudH}} km up, the Sun {{rayElev}}° high, and the camera holds its lens level as it turns. Each beam lies in the plane through the eye, its gap and the Sun's direction, n̂ = ŝ × ĝ / |ŝ × ĝ|: on the sky, a great circle through the Sun and the antisolar point. No distance enters.
rays.verdict: Would refute the picture: anticrepuscular rays that do not converge on the point opposite the Sun, or beams that converge side-on.
near.title: The best fit of the fan: a Sun just above the clouds, and the same picture
near.mini: Reading the fan as if it lay flat in the clouds puts the Sun {{nearD}} km away, {{nearAbove}} m above them. That Sun makes the same fan: one photo of sunbeams gives no distance. Its ground differs: patches {{patchK}}× the gaps.
near.text: The usual way to get the Sun's distance from sunbeams is to assume the fan lies flat in the plane of the clouds. A least-squares fit of the fan's {{fitN}} beams in that plane, {{fitZc}} km away, puts the Sun {{nearD}} km away and {{nearH}} km up, {{nearAbove}} m above the clouds; the fit is perfect, and would be at any assumed distance. Its beams really do spread out, yet from the eye they lie on the same great circles as a distant Sun's, through the Sun and the antisolar point: the fan, the parallel beams side-on and the convergence behind are all there again [1] [2]. Only where each beam ends changes. From above, its shafts spread out from the point under it and its patches of light are the gaps enlarged {{patchK}} times; shadows of posts b apart across the Sun's direction differ by Δψ = b/D, {{spreadNear}}° per km for this Sun. Shadows seen from above across a landscape are parallel, which excludes a Sun a few kilometres away. A Sun {{sunH}} km up would spread them by only {{spreadFlat}}° per km: telling it from a distant Sun takes baselines of hundreds of kilometres.
near.verdict: Would vindicate a close Sun: shadows fanning out from a point across a few kilometres, patches of light larger than their gaps, anticrepuscular rays not centred opposite the Sun.
anti.title: Where anticrepuscular rays meet: a receding Sun against a setting Sun
anti.mini: Anticrepuscular rays meet opposite the Sun, at −α. A Sun receding over a plane never gets below {{alphaMin}}°, so they meet {{alphaMin}}° or more under the horizon. A setting Sun brings their meeting point up through the horizon, into the Earth's shadow.
anti.text: Every anticrepuscular ray lies on a great circle through the Sun and the antisolar point [2], so the rays meet at h_A = −α, as far below the horizon as the Sun is above it. Flat-earth models keep the Sun thousands of kilometres above the disc [1]: as it recedes, α = arctan(H/d) falls only to {{alphaMin}}° at {{dMax}} km, and the meeting point stays {{alphaMin}}° or more below the eastern horizon, in the ground. On a globe the Sun sets: α passes through zero and the meeting point rises through the horizon and into the sky. After sunset it lies inside the Earth's shadow, the blue-grey band rising in the east, under the pink Belt of Venus [3]; anticrepuscular rays photographed at dusk meet there.
anti.verdict: Would vindicate the plane: at dusk, anticrepuscular rays that never meet above the eastern horizon, and no dark band rising there after sunset.
zoom.title: A zoom brings back what perspective shrank, not what the horizon hides
zoom.mini: A zoom multiplies every angle by N; the height hidden behind a curved sea, H = (d − √(2Rh))²/(2R), does not depend on N. On a plane a zoom gives a boat back whole; on a globe its hull stays hidden.
zoom.text: Perspective only divides angles by the distance, so a zoom by the same factor undoes it [1]. A curved sea is different: the water between the eye and the boat hides its lower part, H = (d − √(2Rh))²/(2R), and N appears nowhere in H. A 20 m boat seen from 2 m above the sea: on a plane, every zoom gives it back whole, sitting just below the horizon. On a globe of radius 6,371 km the horizon is {{d0}} km away; at 15 km {{hid15}} m of the boat are hidden ({{hid15k}} m with standard refraction, k = 0.13), and the whole boat is gone at {{sink}} km ({{sinkK}} km with refraction). Zooming in enlarges what is still visible; what is behind the water stays behind it.
zoom.verdict: Would vindicate the flat sea: a hull that a stronger zoom brings back above the horizon, at any distance.
